text.what: Leaves of the Palmyra or talipot palm, cooked, dried and smoke-treated until they take a line. The writing is not laid on the surface but cut into it with a stylus; colouring is then rubbed over the leaf so the pigment settles into the grooves and the letters appear. The result is flexible, light, and cheap wherever the palms grow.
text.story:
Palm leaf carries scripture across half of Asia, and carries charms with it. It is in use in the Indian subcontinent as early as the fifth century BCE and spreads to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia — Cambodia from Angkorian times, Myanmar from twelfth-century Bagan, Indonesia in the Majapahit period of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

In Thailand the takrut, the tubular amulet worn on a cord, is made of metal or of palm leaf: a strip inscribed with yant, the sacred geometry and Pali phrases usually written in Khom script, or in Lan Na Tai Tham in the north, then rolled and cased. Whether a given takrut is metal or leaf is not a difference in the spell. It is a difference in what will survive.

*Inference —* this is the clearest survival-bias case in the atlas. A palm-leaf text lasts between a few decades and roughly six hundred years before moisture, insects, mould and sheer fragility take it, and the oldest survivals are all from colder, drier places — parts of Nepal, Tibet, Central Asia. In the monsoon belt where palm leaf is actually from, nothing lasts. Hindu temples and monasteries handled this by copying texts onto new leaves as the old ones wore out, which keeps the words and destroys the objects. So the amulet record of mainland Southeast Asia is weighted almost entirely to metal, clay and stone, and the leaf charms that stood beside them for two thousand years are simply absent.
text.how: Cut to a strip, inscribed with a stylus, inked or coloured so the grooves show, then rolled and tied, or bound between boards. A takrut of leaf is rolled tight, bound with cord, and often cased so the leaf is never touched.
text.today: Still written, still copied, and now digitised in large collections. As an amulet material it survives mainly in Thai and Khmer practice, alongside the metal sheet that has always been its more durable alternative.

dating.label: c. 500 BCE to now
dating.note: Dated from the earliest reported use of palm leaf for writing in the Indian subcontinent. No surviving leaf is anything like that old; the material's own lifespan is a few decades to about six hundred years.
